questions.question: Why should 'scanf(" %c", &ch)' include a leading space before '%c' when reading a character after numbers?
questions.a: To convert lowercase input into uppercase
questions.b: To skip any leading whitespace characters, including newline left in the buffer by previous input
questions.d: To allocate dynamic memory for the character
questions.explanation: A leading space in a scanf format string instructs scanf to discard any preceding whitespace (such as trailing newlines) before reading.

questions.question: Which standard I/O stream is line-buffered by default when connected to an interactive terminal?
questions.b: stdout
questions.explanation: stdout is typically line-buffered when connected to a terminal (flushing whenever a '\n' is written).

questions.question: Which standard I/O stream is completely unbuffered by default in C?
questions.b: stdout
questions.explanation: stderr is unbuffered by default so that diagnostic error messages appear immediately even if the program crashes.

questions.question: Which standard function can configure the buffering mode (unbuffered, line-buffered, or fully-buffered) of a stream?
questions.b: config_stream()
questions.explanation: setvbuf() allows full control over stream buffering modes (_IONBF, _IOLBF, _IOFBF) and custom buffer pointers.

questions.question: What does 'sscanf(str, ...)' do in C?
questions.a: Reads encrypted secure data from standard input
questions.b: Reads and parses formatted data directly from a character string buffer in memory
questions.c: Writes formatted data to an SSL socket
questions.explanation: sscanf() parses formatted data from an existing null-terminated string buffer rather than a file stream.

questions.question: What does 'sprintf(buffer, ...)' do in C?
questions.a: Prints formatted output directly to the terminal screen
questions.b: Writes formatted output into a character array buffer in memory
questions.c: Measures the printing speed of I/O streams
questions.explanation: sprintf() composes formatted strings and writes the resulting characters into a destination string buffer.

questions.question: Why is 'snprintf()' safer than 'sprintf()'?
questions.b: snprintf takes a buffer size argument to prevent buffer overrun / buffer overflow vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: snprintf(buf, max_size, fmt, ...) guarantees that no more than max_size bytes (including '\0') are written to the buffer.

questions.question: What value is returned by 'getchar()' when an error occurs or End-Of-File is encountered?
questions.b: -1 (represented by macro EOF)
questions.explanation: getchar() returns EOF (defined as -1 in <stdio.h>) on end-of-file or stream read errors.

questions.question: Why must the return value of 'getchar()' be stored in an 'int' variable rather than a 'char'?
questions.a: Because char is faster to process than int on modern 64-bit systems
questions.b: Because EOF is an int value (-1) that may not fit or may be indistinguishable from a valid byte in unsigned char
questions.d: Because char variables cannot be passed to printf
questions.explanation: EOF (-1) cannot be reliably represented by an unsigned char (where it converts to 255), causing potential infinite read loops.

questions.question: What does the format specifier '%*d' do in a scanf() format string?
questions.b: Reads and suppresses (discards) the matching integer without assigning it to any variable
questions.c: Reads a pointer to an integer
questions.explanation: The asterisk '*' in a scanf conversion specifier acts as an assignment-suppression flag, skipping the matched field.

questions.question: What does 'feof(stream)' return when the end of the file/stream has been reached?
questions.b: A non-zero value
questions.explanation: feof() returns non-zero if the end-of-file indicator has been set for the given stream after an attempted read.

questions.question: What does a function return type of void signify?
questions.a: The function returns a generic void* pointer
questions.b: The function does not return any value to caller
questions.c: The function terminates the entire program
questions.d: The function takes no parameter arguments
questions.explanation: void as return type indicates that no value is returned to the caller.

questions.question: What is the default argument passing mechanism in C functions?
questions.b: Pass by value
questions.explanation: C exclusively uses pass-by-value; copies of arguments are passed to function parameters.

questions.question: What is a function prototype (forward declaration)?
questions.a: The complete machine code compiled binary
questions.b: A declaration informing the compiler of function signature before definition
questions.c: A macro that replaces function calls inline
questions.d: A special function that executes before main()
questions.explanation: Prototypes declare name, parameters, and return type so the compiler can validate calls before full definition.

questions.question: What happens to a local variable declared inside a function when the function returns?
questions.a: It is persisted permanently in global static memory
questions.b: Its stack frame memory is reclaimed and destroyed
questions.c: It is automatically migrated into heap storage
questions.d: It remains accessible through its original name
questions.explanation: Automatic local variables have automatic storage duration on the stack and expire upon function exit.

questions.question: What is the effect of declaring a local variable with the static keyword inside a function?
questions.a: It retains its value across multiple function calls
questions.b: It makes the variable immutable like a constant
questions.c: It allocates the variable on the runtime heap
questions.d: It allows other source files to access the variable
questions.explanation: static local variables are initialized once and preserve state between successive function invocations.

questions.question: What must every recursive function contain to avoid infinite recursion and stack overflow?
questions.a: At least one dynamic malloc allocation call
questions.b: A base case condition that terminates recursion
questions.c: A loop statement iterating over arguments
questions.d: A static local counter variable definition
questions.explanation: A base case returns without making further recursive calls, preventing stack overflow.

questions.question: What is a 'Function Prototype' (forward declaration) in C?
questions.a: The compiled binary of a function
questions.b: A declaration specifying the function's name, return type, and parameter types before its actual definition
questions.explanation: Prototypes inform the compiler of function signatures before call sites occur.

questions.question: In C, are function arguments passed by value or by reference by default?
questions.b: Pass by Value (a local copy of each argument is created in the function's stack frame)
questions.explanation: C exclusively uses pass-by-value; pass-by-reference is simulated by passing pointer addresses.

questions.question: What does the 'static' storage class specifier do when applied to a local variable inside a function?
questions.b: Preserves the variable's value across multiple function calls, maintaining static lifetime throughout program execution
questions.explanation: Static local variables retain their values across function invocations throughout program lifetime.

questions.question: What does the 'static' keyword do when applied to a global function or variable at file scope?
questions.a: Restricts its linkage and visibility strictly to that translation unit (file), preventing external access
questions.b: Makes it thread-safe
questions.c: Exports it to all C files
questions.explanation: Internal linkage (static) hides functions and global variables from other source files.

questions.question: What is 'Recursion' in C programming?
questions.b: A programming technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems until reaching a base case
questions.explanation: Recursive functions call themselves until satisfying terminating base conditions.

questions.question: What fatal error occurs if a recursive function lacks a proper base case or recurses too deeply?
questions.a: Segmentation fault due to Stack Overflow (call stack exhaustion)
questions.b: Heap corruption
questions.explanation: Unbounded recursion exhausts stack memory allocation, triggering stack overflow crashes.

questions.question: What does the 'inline' function specifier suggest to the C compiler?
questions.b: Suggests replacing function calls with the actual body code to eliminate call overhead
questions.d: Force function to run in kernel mode
questions.explanation: inline advises the compiler to inline code at call sites to eliminate call frame overhead.

questions.question: What is the return type of a function that does not return any value?
questions.b: void
questions.explanation: void denotes an absence of return value.

questions.question: Which standard header defines macros for handling variable-argument functions (variadic functions like printf)?
questions.b: <varargs.h>
questions.explanation: <stdarg.h> provides va_list, va_start, va_arg, and va_end macros.

questions.question: What is a 'Pure Function' in software design?
questions.a: A function written without any comments
questions.b: A function whose return value depends solely on its input arguments, producing no observable side effects
questions.explanation: Pure functions produce deterministic output from inputs without mutating global state.

questions.question: What is the purpose of passing arguments to a function via pointers in C?
questions.a: To convert the arguments into global variables
questions.b: To allow the function to modify the caller's actual arguments (pass-by-reference simulation) and avoid copying large structures
questions.c: To execute the function asynchronously in parallel
questions.explanation: Passing pointers allows functions to mutate variables in the caller scope and improves performance for large data objects.

questions.question: What happens if a non-void function reaches the end of its body without executing a 'return' statement in C99?
questions.b: Reaching the end of a non-void function (other than main) and attempting to use its return value invokes Undefined Behavior
questions.d: The compiler will not allow the code to compile under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Flowing off the end of a value-returning function (except main in C99+) invokes undefined behavior if the caller uses the return value.

questions.question: What does the 'extern' storage class specifier signify in a variable or function declaration?
questions.a: The variable is stored on the external USB storage
questions.b: The variable or function is defined in another source file or translation unit and linked globally
questions.c: The variable has thread-local storage duration
questions.d: The function cannot accept any arguments
questions.explanation: 'extern' declares an identifier with external linkage, referencing an object or function defined elsewhere in the program.

questions.question: What is a 'variadic function' in C?
questions.a: A function that can return multiple values simultaneously
questions.b: A function that accepts a variable number of arguments (e.g. printf)
questions.c: A function that changes its algorithm at runtime
questions.d: A function declared inside another function body
questions.explanation: Variadic functions take an arbitrary number of parameters, declared with an ellipsis '...' and accessed via <stdarg.h> macros.

questions.question: Which macro from <stdarg.h> initializes a 'va_list' variable to retrieve variadic arguments?
questions.b: va_arg()
questions.explanation: va_start(ap, last_named_arg) initializes the va_list argument pointer.

questions.question: Which macro from <stdarg.h> cleans up resources associated with a 'va_list' variable before returning from a variadic function?
questions.b: va_arg()
questions.explanation: va_end(ap) must be called to finalize and cleanup a va_list object before function exit.

questions.question: What is 'Block Scope' (lexical scope) in C?
questions.a: Identifiers are visible only within the enclosing pair of braces { } where they are declared
questions.b: Variables are visible across all hard drive storage blocks
questions.c: Functions are accessible only by the operating system kernel
questions.d: Variables remain in memory after the program terminates
questions.explanation: Block scope limits visibility of variables to the compound statement '{ ... }' in which they are declared.

questions.question: What is 'Variable Shadowing' (name hiding) in C?
questions.a: Encrypting variable names in the binary
questions.b: Declaring a variable in an inner scope with the same identifier as a variable in an outer scope, hiding the outer variable
questions.c: Creating duplicate pointers to the same memory address
questions.d: Saving backup copies of variables on the stack
questions.explanation: Shadowing occurs when an inner block variable hides an outer block variable of the same name within its scope.

questions.question: What is a 'Tail-Recursive' function?
questions.a: A recursive function that executes without any base case
questions.b: A recursive function where the recursive call is the very last operation performed before returning
questions.c: A function that recurses inside a while loop header
questions.d: A function that alternates between two helper functions
questions.explanation: In tail recursion, the recursive call is the final action in the function, allowing compilers to optimize it into a loop (Tail Call Optimization).

questions.question: What is the 'call stack' used for during function execution in C?
questions.a: Storing dynamic heap memory allocated via malloc()
questions.b: Storing activation records (stack frames) containing return addresses, parameters, and local variables
questions.explanation: The call stack manages stack frames containing return addresses, function parameters, and automatic local variables.

questions.question: Can C functions be declared inside the body of another function (nested functions) in standard ISO C?
questions.a: Yes, standard C fully supports nested functions
questions.b: No, standard ISO C does not support nested function definitions (though GCC has a non-standard extension)
questions.d: Only if declared as static inline
questions.explanation: Standard ISO C forbids nested function definitions; all functions must be defined at file/global scope.

questions.question: What is the 'register' storage class specifier hint intended for in C?
questions.a: Storing the variable in a database
questions.b: Suggesting to the compiler to store the variable in a fast CPU register instead of RAM
questions.c: Registering the function with the OS kernel
questions.d: Preventing variables from being garbage collected
questions.explanation: 'register' hints that a variable will be heavily accessed and should reside in a CPU register (address-of '&' operator cannot be applied to it).

questions.question: What is the lifetime (storage duration) of a local 'static' variable inside a function in C?
questions.a: It exists only during the function's execution and is destroyed upon return
questions.b: It persists throughout the entire execution lifetime of the program, retaining its value between function calls
questions.c: It persists until the caller function returns
questions.d: It exists only while CPU cache is active
questions.explanation: Static local variables have static storage duration: they are initialized once and persist for the entire program run.

questions.question: What is the return type of the function declaration: 'int *create_array(int size)'?
questions.b: A pointer to an integer (int *)
questions.explanation: The return type is 'int *', meaning the function returns the memory address of an integer or array of integers.

questions.question: What does the & operator return when placed before a variable name?
questions.a: The value stored in the variable
questions.b: The memory address of the variable
questions.c: The size of the variable in bytes
questions.d: A pointer to the next array element
questions.explanation: The & (address-of) operator yields the physical memory location of an lvalue.

questions.question: What operation is performed by *ptr when ptr is a pointer holding a valid memory address?
questions.b: Dereferencing to access value at address
questions.d: Incrementing the address stored in ptr
questions.explanation: The unary * operator dereferences a pointer, reading or modifying the value stored at the pointed address.

questions.question: If ptr points to an int on a system with 4-byte integers, what does ptr + 1 point to?
questions.b: 4 bytes after ptr
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic scales by sizeof(type). ptr + 1 advances the address by sizeof(int) = 4 bytes.

questions.question: What does malloc() return if the operating system has insufficient memory to satisfy the request?
questions.b: NULL
questions.d: A pointer to swap disk space
questions.explanation: malloc returns NULL upon allocation failure. Code should always verify ptr != NULL before use.

questions.question: What is the critical difference between malloc() and calloc()?
questions.a: malloc() allocates on stack; calloc() allocates on heap
questions.b: calloc() initializes allocated memory to zero; malloc() does not
questions.c: malloc() is faster because it automatically frees memory
questions.d: calloc() can only allocate character array memory blocks
questions.explanation: calloc(n, size) clears all allocated bytes to zero; malloc(size) leaves memory uninitialized.

questions.question: What is a dangling pointer?
questions.a: A pointer initialized to NULL address
questions.b: A pointer referencing memory that has been freed
questions.c: A pointer pointing to a global variable
questions.d: A void pointer with no associated data type
questions.explanation: A dangling pointer holds the address of deallocated or out-of-scope memory.

questions.question: What does the dereference operator '*' do when applied to a pointer variable (e.g. '*ptr')?
questions.b: Accesses or modifies the value stored at the memory address pointed to by the pointer
questions.c: Gets the address of the pointer itself
questions.explanation: *ptr accesses the target data value at the referenced memory address.

questions.question: What is a 'NULL' pointer in C?
questions.a: A pointer pointing to random heap data
questions.b: A pointer assigned a special reserved value (address 0) indicating it does not point to any valid memory object
questions.c: A pointer to a character array
questions.explanation: NULL indicates a non-pointing reference. Dereferencing NULL causes instant segmentation faults.

questions.question: What is a 'Dangling Pointer' in C memory management?
questions.a: A pointer pointing to a memory location that has already been deallocated (freed)
questions.b: A pointer with a value of NULL
questions.explanation: Dangling pointers reference invalidated memory, causing critical use-after-free bugs.

questions.question: What does Pointer Arithmetic 'ptr + 1' do on a pointer of type 'int *' (assuming 4-byte integers)?
questions.a: Adds 1 byte to the memory address
questions.b: Advances the memory address by sizeof(int) (4 bytes) to point to the next contiguous integer
questions.d: Increments the integer value stored at ptr
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic scales automatically by the byte size of the underlying target data type.

questions.question: What is a 'Void Pointer' (void *) in C?
questions.a: A pointer that cannot point to anything
questions.b: A generic, typeless pointer that can hold the memory address of any data type without type casting
questions.c: A pointer to a function returning void
questions.explanation: void * is a universal generic pointer type used in memory functions like malloc and memcpy.

questions.question: Which dynamic memory allocation function allocates a contiguous block of bytes from the heap WITHOUT initializing them?
questions.b: malloc()
questions.explanation: malloc(size) allocates uninitialized heap memory containing indeterminate garbage bytes.

questions.question: Which dynamic memory allocation function allocates memory and zeroes out all allocated bytes?
questions.b: malloc()
questions.explanation: calloc() allocates memory and initializes all bytes to zero.

questions.question: What is a 'Memory Leak' in C?
questions.b: When dynamically allocated heap memory (via malloc/calloc) is no longer referenced but never released with free(), consuming available RAM
questions.d: When a file is deleted from hard disk
questions.explanation: Memory leaks occur when allocated heap blocks are abandoned without calling free().

questions.question: What is the consequence of 'Double Free' (calling free() twice on the same memory pointer)?
questions.a: It frees the memory twice as fast
questions.b: It causes heap corruption and Undefined Behavior, often leading to security exploits or immediate crash
questions.explanation: Double free corrupts heap allocator metadata and is a major security vulnerability.

questions.question: What is a 'Function Pointer' in C?
questions.a: A pointer pointing to a variable in main()
questions.b: A pointer that stores the memory address of executable code (a function) allowing dynamic callback invocation
questions.c: A function that returns a pointer
questions.explanation: Function pointers store code addresses and enable callbacks and runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: What does the declaration 'const int *ptr' mean in C?
questions.a: The pointer 'ptr' is constant and cannot point to a different address
questions.b: The integer value pointed to by 'ptr' cannot be modified through this pointer (pointer to const int)
questions.c: Both the pointer and the integer value are unmodifiable
questions.d: The pointer is allocated in read-only hardware ROM
questions.explanation: 'const int *ptr' denotes a pointer to a constant integer: the pointed-to data is read-only through ptr, but ptr itself can point elsewhere.

questions.question: What does the declaration 'int * const ptr' mean in C?
questions.a: The pointer 'ptr' is constant and cannot be changed to point to another memory address (const pointer to int)
questions.b: The integer value pointed to is read-only
questions.c: The pointer must point to a global variable only
questions.explanation: 'int * const ptr' means the pointer address itself is immutable (constant pointer), but the integer value it points to can be modified.

questions.question: What is a 'Wild Pointer' in C?
questions.a: A pointer that points to another pointer
questions.b: An uninitialized pointer holding an arbitrary/garbage memory address
questions.c: A pointer that dynamically reallocates memory
questions.d: A function pointer pointing to an assembly routine
questions.explanation: A wild pointer is an uninitialized pointer that points to an unpredictable memory address, risking memory corruption if dereferenced.

questions.question: What is the size of any pointer variable (e.g. char*, int*, double*) on a standard 64-bit operating system architecture?
questions.b: 4 bytes
questions.explanation: On 64-bit architectures, memory addresses are 64 bits wide, making all pointer types occupy 8 bytes.

questions.question: What is the result of subtracting two pointers 'p2 - p1' that point to elements of the same array?
questions.a: The difference in bytes divided by the size of the pointed-to element type (ptrdiff_t index difference)
questions.b: The physical RAM memory difference in raw bits
questions.c: A new pointer pointing to the middle of the array
questions.explanation: Pointer subtraction yields the number of elements separating the two pointers, represented as type 'ptrdiff_t'.

questions.question: Which standard header defines the signed integer type 'ptrdiff_t'?
questions.b: <stddef.h>
questions.explanation: <stddef.h> defines 'ptrdiff_t' alongside 'size_t', 'wchar_t', and 'NULL'.

questions.question: What is a 'pointer to pointer' (double pointer, e.g. 'int **pptr')?
questions.a: A pointer that points to two memory locations simultaneously
questions.b: A variable that holds the memory address of another pointer variable
questions.c: A pointer allocated on the dual-channel memory bus
questions.d: A pointer that dereferences twice as fast
questions.explanation: A double pointer holds the memory address of another pointer variable, widely used for modifying caller pointer values and dynamic 2D arrays.

questions.question: Can arithmetic operations like addition (+) or multiplication (*) be performed on two pointers directly (e.g. 'ptr1 + ptr2')?
questions.b: No, adding or multiplying two pointers is illegal and causes a compile-time error
questions.c: Yes, but only in kernel drivers
questions.d: Only if both pointers are void*
questions.explanation: Adding two pointers is mathematically meaningless in memory addressing and is forbidden by C syntax (only pointer +/- integer or pointer - pointer is valid).

questions.question: What is the effect of casting a pointer to 'void *' and back to its original pointer type in C?
questions.b: The pointer value is preserved unchanged (safe round-trip conversion)
questions.c: It frees the underlying heap memory
questions.d: It invalidates all CPU cache lines
questions.explanation: C guarantees that converting any object pointer to void* and back to the original pointer type yields the exact original pointer value.

questions.question: Why can you not directly dereference a 'void *' pointer (e.g. '*vptr') in standard ISO C?
questions.a: Because void pointers are always NULL
questions.b: Because void has an incomplete type with no known size, so the compiler cannot determine how many bytes to read or write
questions.c: Because void pointers only exist during compile time
questions.d: Because void pointers are stored in GPU VRAM
questions.explanation: void has no size, so dereferencing void* requires first casting it to a concrete object pointer type (e.g., int* or char*).

questions.question: What should you set a pointer variable to immediately after calling 'free(ptr)' to prevent use-after-free bugs?
questions.b: ptr = NULL;
questions.explanation: Setting ptr = NULL after freeing ensures that subsequent attempts to use or free ptr can be detected safely (free(NULL) is a safe no-op).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'alignof' operator (or _Alignof in C11)?
questions.a: To align text strings to the right
questions.b: To determine the memory byte alignment requirement of a specified data type
questions.c: To calculate pointer offset in structs
questions.d: To align loops to cache boundaries
questions.explanation: C11's _Alignof (alignof in <stdalign.h>) returns the alignment requirement in bytes for a given type.

questions.question: What is a 'Use-After-Free' security vulnerability?
questions.a: Using RAM after uninstalling the software
questions.b: Accessing or modifying heap memory through a dangling pointer after that memory block has already been deallocated by free()
questions.c: Calling malloc() without checking the return value
questions.d: Allocating memory inside a recursive loop
questions.explanation: Use-after-free occurs when an application accesses memory via a pointer that has been freed, enabling arbitrary code execution exploits.

questions.question: How do you invoke a function using a function pointer 'void (*fp)(int)' with argument 10 in C?
questions.explanation: Both 'fp(10)' and '(*fp)(10)' are standard and valid syntax in C to invoke the function referenced by function pointer fp.

questions.question: How do you access a structure member through a pointer struct Student *s?
questions.b: s->name
questions.explanation: The arrow operator s->name is syntactic shorthand for (*s).name.

questions.question: What is the primary memory difference between struct and union in C?
questions.a: Struct members share memory; union members are separate
questions.b: Union members share same memory; struct members are separate
questions.c: Structs are allocated on heap; unions are on stack
questions.d: Unions cannot store pointer data type members
questions.explanation: In union, all members overlay the same memory space (size = largest member). Struct members have separate offsets.

questions.question: Which fopen() mode opens a file for writing, discarding existing content or creating a new file?
questions.explanation: "w" opens for writing and truncates existing file content to zero length or creates a new file.

questions.question: What does fopen() return when the specified file path cannot be opened?
questions.b: NULL
questions.explanation: fopen() returns a NULL pointer if it fails to open or create the file.

questions.question: What does typedef do in C?
questions.a: Allocates a new structure on heap storage
questions.b: Creates an alias name for an existing data type
questions.c: Restricts variable mutation like const qualifier
questions.d: Imports external types from external headers
questions.explanation: typedef creates synonym aliases for existing types (e.g. typedef unsigned long ulong;).

questions.question: What is the default integer value assigned to the first identifier in an enum if unassigned?
questions.explanation: Enum constants start at 0 by default and increment by 1 for each subsequent member.

questions.question: Which function must always be called to flush buffers and release file handles opened with fopen()?
questions.b: fclose()
questions.explanation: fclose(fp) flushes internal stream buffers and closes OS file descriptor handles.

questions.question: Which operator is used to access struct members through a pointer to that struct (e.g. 'ptr->member')?
questions.b: Arrow operator (->)
questions.explanation: Arrow operator 'ptr->x' is shorthand for '(*ptr).x'.

questions.question: What is 'Structure Padding' in C memory alignment?
questions.a: Adding comments inside a struct definition
questions.b: Unused bytes inserted by the compiler between struct members to align data types with natural hardware word boundaries for fast CPU access
questions.c: Compressing struct members to save disk space
questions.explanation: Compilers insert padding bytes so members align with CPU word boundaries (e.g. 4 or 8 bytes).

questions.question: What is the key difference between a 'struct' and a 'union' in C?
questions.a: In a struct, each member has its own separate memory; in a union, all members share the exact same memory location (size equals largest member)
questions.b: Unions can only hold integers
questions.d: There is no difference in ISO C
questions.explanation: Unions overlay all member fields over the same shared memory offset.

questions.question: Which standard library function opens a file stream in C?
questions.b: fopen(filename, mode)
questions.explanation: fopen() opens a file and returns a FILE * stream handle, or NULL on failure.

questions.question: What does the file open mode '"rb"' specify in fopen()?
questions.a: Open file for writing in text mode
questions.b: Open an existing file for reading in binary mode
questions.explanation: "rb" opens an existing binary file for input reading without newline translation.

questions.question: Which function writes raw binary blocks of memory directly to a file stream?
questions.b: fwrite(ptr, size, count, stream)
questions.explanation: fwrite() writes raw binary buffers to streams.

questions.question: Which function reads raw binary data from a file stream into a memory buffer?
questions.b: fscanf()
questions.explanation: fread() reads binary records from a file stream directly into memory.

questions.question: Which function repositions the file position indicator in a file stream to a specific byte offset?
questions.b: ftell()
questions.explanation: fseek() moves the stream file pointer relative to SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, or SEEK_END.

questions.question: What does 'ftell(stream)' return?
questions.a: The current byte position offset of the file indicator from the beginning of the file
questions.b: Total number of lines in the file
questions.explanation: ftell() reports the current file position offset in bytes.

questions.question: Why must 'fclose(stream)' always be called when file I/O operations are finished?
questions.a: To prevent file system corruption, flush cached output buffers, and release OS file descriptor handles
questions.b: To delete the file from disk
questions.d: It is optional and does nothing
questions.explanation: Closing files flushes remaining buffer caches and releases OS handle resources.

questions.question: What is the 'offsetof' macro from <stddef.h> used for in C?
questions.a: Computing the offset in bytes of a struct member from the beginning of the struct
questions.b: Calculating file pointer offset from EOF
questions.explanation: offsetof(type, member) returns the byte offset of a structure member from the start of the struct.

questions.question: What is a 'Bit-field' in a C struct declaration (e.g. 'unsigned int flag : 1;')?
questions.b: A structure member allocated with an explicit, fixed number of bits to pack data tightly
questions.d: A field stored in CPU registers
questions.explanation: Bit-fields allow struct members to occupy a specified number of bits, optimizing storage for hardware registers and protocols.

questions.question: What is a 'Flexible Array Member' in C99 structs (e.g. 'struct Packet { int len; char data[]; };')?
questions.a: An array that automatically resizes like a C++ vector
questions.b: An unsized array declared as the last member of a struct to allow dynamic variable-length payload allocation
questions.c: A linked list embedded inside a struct
questions.d: A pointer to a stack array
questions.explanation: C99 flexible array members allow the last member of a struct to have incomplete array type, allocating tail payloads in a single malloc call.

questions.question: What does the file open mode '"a+"' (or '"a+b"') specify in fopen()?
questions.b: Open for both reading and appending (all writes go to the end of the file, creating file if absent)
questions.c: Truncate existing file and open for write
questions.explanation: 'a+' opens the file for reading and appending. Output operations always append data to the end of the file.

questions.question: What does 'fseek(file_ptr, 0, SEEK_END)' do?
questions.a: Resets the file position indicator to the beginning of the file
questions.b: Moves the file position indicator directly to the end of the file
questions.c: Deletes the contents of the file
questions.d: Returns the size of the file
questions.explanation: fseek with SEEK_END and offset 0 positions the stream indicator at the very end of the file (often combined with ftell() to get file size).

questions.question: What does the macro 'SEEK_SET' specify when passed as the whence argument to fseek()?
questions.a: Offset relative to the start of the file
questions.b: Offset relative to the current position indicator
questions.c: Offset relative to the end of the file
questions.d: Offset relative to disk sector zero
questions.explanation: SEEK_SET indicates that the offset is calculated relative to the start of the file (byte 0).

questions.question: What does the 'rewind(stream)' function do in C standard file I/O?
questions.b: Sets the file position indicator to the beginning of the file and clears error indicators (equivalent to (void)fseek(s, 0L, SEEK_SET); clearerr(s);)
questions.c: Reverses the byte order of the file
questions.explanation: rewind(stream) resets the file position to byte 0 and clears stream error/EOF flags.

questions.question: What does 'perror("Error opening file")' do in C?
questions.a: Terminates the program immediately with an abort signal
questions.b: Prints the custom message followed by the human-readable description of the current 'errno' to stderr
questions.c: Writes error messages to a system log file on disk
questions.explanation: perror() prints the specified string followed by a colon and the error message corresponding to global errno to stderr.

questions.question: Which standard header defines the global variable 'errno' and system error code macros like ENOENT, ENOMEM, EACCES?
questions.b: <errno.h>
questions.explanation: <errno.h> defines the integer lvalue errno and symbolic integer error constants.

questions.question: What is an 'Anonymous Union' inside a struct in modern C (C11)?
questions.a: A union without a tag or member name whose fields are directly accessible as members of the outer struct
questions.b: A union that cannot be modified
questions.c: A union that stores untyped void pointers
questions.d: A union declared inside a macro
questions.explanation: C11 anonymous unions/structs allow their members to be accessed directly without an intermediate member name.

questions.question: What does the function 'remove("filename.txt")' from <stdio.h> do?
questions.b: Deletes the specified file from the filesystem
questions.c: Removes all formatting from the file
questions.d: Truncates the file to 0 bytes without deleting it
questions.explanation: remove(filename) deletes the file identified by the path from the filesystem.

questions.question: What does the function 'rename("old.txt", "new.txt")' do in C?
questions.b: Renames or moves the file from old.txt to new.txt
questions.d: Compares the names of the two files
questions.explanation: rename(oldname, newname) renames the file or moves it across directories within the same filesystem.

questions.question: Can an enum in C have explicitly assigned values (e.g. enum State { OFF = 0, ON = 5, PAUSED = 10 };)?
questions.a: No, enums must always be contiguous starting from 0
questions.b: Yes, any enum identifier can be explicitly initialized to an arbitrary integer constant
questions.explanation: Enum identifiers can be assigned custom integer values. Subsequent unassigned identifiers increment from the previous value.

questions.question: Which header file must be included to use functions like sqrt(), pow(), and ceil()?
questions.b: <math.h>
questions.explanation: The <math.h> header contains declarations for standard mathematical functions in C.

questions.question: What is the return value of the function call ceil(4.2)?
questions.explanation: The ceil() function rounds a floating-point number UP to the nearest integer.

questions.question: How does the floor() function behave when given a negative number like -3.4?
questions.b: Returns -4.0
questions.explanation: floor() rounds DOWN to the nearest integer. For negative numbers, rounding down moves further away from zero.

questions.question: Which operator is used to access a member of a struct variable directly (not through a pointer)?
questions.explanation: The dot (.) operator accesses members of a standard struct variable, while the arrow (->) is used for struct pointers.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to declare an array of 10 'Student' structs?
questions.b: struct Student arr[10];
questions.explanation: In C, you combine the struct keyword, the tag name (Student), the variable name (arr), and the array size [10].

questions.question: If 'arr' is an integer array, what is the pointer arithmetic equivalent of accessing arr[2]?
questions.explanation: In C, the array name acts as a pointer to its first element. *(arr + 2) dereferences the address two integer spaces ahead of the base.

questions.question: Which function allows you to safely resize a previously allocated block of dynamic memory?
questions.b: resize()
questions.explanation: realloc() changes the size of a previously allocated memory block, moving it to a new location if necessary to find contiguous space.

questions.question: What happens if realloc() fails to find enough contiguous memory to expand a block?
questions.b: It returns NULL and leaves the original memory block untouched
questions.c: It automatically deletes the old block and returns NULL
questions.d: It returns a pointer to the hard drive's swap space
questions.explanation: If realloc fails, it returns NULL. Developers must check for NULL before overwriting the original pointer to avoid memory leaks.

questions.question: Which function is used to write formatted text data to a file stream?
questions.b: fwrite()
questions.explanation: fprintf() operates exactly like printf(), but requires a file pointer as its first argument to direct the output to a file.

questions.question: When reading from a file using fgetc(), what special macro represents the end of the file?
questions.explanation: EOF (End Of File) is a macro defined in <stdio.h> (usually as -1) returned when there is no more data to read.

questions.question: Which function allows you to read an entire line of text from a file safely into a buffer?
questions.b: fgets()
questions.explanation: fgets() reads up to a specified number of characters from a file stream, stopping at a newline or EOF, preventing buffer overflows.

questions.question: Which standard library function dynamically changes the size of previously allocated heap memory?
questions.b: realloc(ptr, new_size)
questions.explanation: realloc() expands or contracts existing heap allocations, migrating data if necessary.

questions.question: What is the safe idiom for realloc() to prevent memory leaks if realloc() fails and returns NULL?
questions.a: Assign directly to original pointer: 'ptr = realloc(ptr, new_size);'
questions.b: Use a temporary pointer: 'void *tmp = realloc(ptr, new_size); if (tmp) ptr = tmp;'
questions.explanation: If realloc fails, assigning directly to ptr overwrites the pointer with NULL, leaking the original block.

questions.question: Which standard header must be included to use mathematical functions like sqrt(), pow(), and sin()?
questions.b: <math.h>
questions.explanation: <math.h> declares standard floating-point trigonometric and algebraic functions.

questions.question: When compiling a C program using <math.h> with GCC on Linux/Unix, which linker flag must be passed?
questions.b: -lmath
questions.explanation: -lm instructs the linker to link the system math library (libm.so/libm.a).

questions.question: Which function computes the square root of a double value in C?
questions.b: sqrt()
questions.explanation: sqrt(x) computes the non-negative square root of x.

questions.question: What does 'pow(2.0, 3.0)' evaluate to in <math.h>?
questions.explanation: pow(x, y) raises x to the power y (2^3 = 8.0).

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> rounds a floating-point number UP to the nearest integer?
questions.b: ceil()
questions.explanation: ceil(3.2) returns 4.0 (smallest integer greater than or equal to x).

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> rounds a floating-point number DOWN to the nearest integer?
questions.b: ceil()
questions.explanation: floor(3.8) returns 3.0 (largest integer less than or equal to x).

questions.question: Which function computes the absolute value of an integer in <stdlib.h>?
questions.b: abs()
questions.explanation: abs() is for integers (<stdlib.h>); fabs() is for floating-point doubles (<math.h>).

questions.question: What does 'qsort()' from <stdlib.h> require as its 4th argument?
questions.b: A pointer to a comparator function: 'int (*compar)(const void *, const void *)'
questions.explanation: qsort() is a generic quicksort routine taking a comparator callback.

questions.question: What is the return value of 'fmod(5.5, 2.0)' from <math.h>?
questions.explanation: fmod(x, y) returns the floating-point remainder of x / y (5.5 = 2.0 * 2 + 1.5).

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> computes the natural logarithm (base e) of a double value?
questions.b: log()
questions.explanation: log(x) computes the natural logarithm ln(x), while log10(x) computes base-10 logarithm.

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> computes the base-2 logarithm of a number in C99?
questions.b: log2()
questions.explanation: log2() was introduced in C99 to compute base-2 logarithms of floating-point values.

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> computes the hypotenuse 'sqrt(x*x + y*y)' without intermediate overflow or underflow?
questions.b: pythagoras()
questions.explanation: hypot(x, y) computes the Euclidean distance safely avoiding overflow in intermediate squaring steps.

questions.question: What function from <stdlib.h> performs a binary search on a sorted array of elements?
questions.b: bsearch()
questions.explanation: bsearch() searches a sorted array for a key matching a comparator function in O(log N) time.

questions.question: What is the return type of the comparison function required by 'qsort()' and 'bsearch()'?
questions.b: int (<0 for less, 0 for equal, >0 for greater)
questions.explanation: The comparator must return an int indicating whether the first element is less than (<0), equal to (0), or greater than (>0) the second.

questions.question: Which standard function generates pseudo-random integer numbers in <stdlib.h>?
questions.b: rand()
questions.explanation: rand() returns a pseudo-random integer in the range [0, RAND_MAX].

questions.question: Which function seeds the pseudo-random number generator in <stdlib.h>?
questions.b: srand()
questions.explanation: srand(unsigned int seed) sets the starting seed for subsequent calls to rand() (commonly initialized with srand(time(NULL))).

questions.question: What function in <math.h> computes the cube root of a double precision number?
questions.b: cubert()
questions.explanation: cbrt(x) computes the cube root of x in C99 and later.

questions.question: What programming paradigm does standard C strictly follow?
questions.b: Functional Programming
questions.explanation: C is a procedural language; it executes sequences of statements, manipulating state directly via functions and variables.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of the standard C compilation pipeline?
questions.b: Preprocessor -> Compiler -> Assembler -> Linker
questions.explanation: The pipeline runs: Preprocessor (handles # directives), Compiler (translates to assembly), Assembler (translates to machine code), Linker (combines object files).

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a compilation error and a runtime error?
questions.a: Compilation errors happen on Windows; runtime errors happen on Linux
questions.b: Compilation errors prevent the executable from being created; runtime errors crash the executable while it is running
questions.c: Compilation errors are caused by hardware; runtime errors are caused by software
questions.explanation: Syntax issues cause compilation errors. Logic flaws (like dividing by zero or bad pointers) cause runtime errors after the program starts.

questions.question: Where are local, non-static variables stored during a function's execution?
questions.b: The Stack
questions.explanation: Local variables with automatic storage duration are pushed onto the Call Stack and are destroyed when the function returns.

questions.question: What does 'endianness' refer to in computer architecture?
questions.a: The maximum memory limit of a C program
questions.b: The byte order used to store multi-byte data types in memory
questions.c: The speed of the CPU cache
questions.d: The process of closing file streams
questions.explanation: Endianness (Big-Endian vs Little-Endian) determines whether the most significant or least significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address.

questions.question: What is an algorithm in the context of programming?
questions.b: A step-by-step set of operations to solve a specific problem
questions.d: A tool used strictly for finding bugs
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a finite sequence of rigorous instructions, independent of any specific programming language.

questions.question: In standard ASCII representation, how is character data actually stored in computer memory?
questions.b: As numeric integer values ranging from 0 to 127
questions.explanation: Computers only understand numbers. ASCII maps characters to integers (e.g., 'A' is stored as the integer 65).

questions.question: Why do C programmers frequently use hexadecimal (Base-16) notation for memory addresses and bitwise masks?
questions.a: It executes faster on modern processors
questions.b: It is the only format the compiler understands
questions.c: It maps perfectly to binary, where one hex digit represents exactly four binary bits
questions.d: It consumes less memory space on the heap
questions.explanation: Hexadecimal is a highly readable shorthand for binary. One hex digit (0-F) perfectly represents a 4-bit nibble (0000-1111).

questions.question: What is the smallest addressable unit of memory in a standard modern computer architecture?
questions.b: Byte
questions.explanation: While a bit is the smallest data unit, a byte (8 bits) is the smallest unit of memory that has its own address in C.

questions.question: What defines a 'side effect' in a programming expression?
questions.a: When an expression calculates a value but fails to return it
questions.b: When a function modifies some state outside its local environment, like a global variable or I/O stream
questions.c: When a program crashes due to a segmentation fault
questions.d: When a compiler optimization ignores unused variables
questions.explanation: A side effect occurs when an expression changes the observable state of the program, such as modifying a file, printing to the screen, or changing a global variable.

questions.question: What are 'Header Guards' (#ifndef HEADER_H, #define HEADER_H, #endif) used for in C?
questions.b: To prevent multiple redundant inclusions of the same header file during preprocessing
questions.d: To speed up runtime CPU execution
questions.explanation: Header guards prevent redefinition errors when headers are included transitively.

questions.question: What is '#pragma once' in modern C compilers?
questions.a: A non-standard but universally supported preprocessor directive serving as a concise header guard
questions.b: A command to compile the file only once in lifetime
questions.explanation: #pragma once ensures the compiler includes the header file only once per translation unit.

questions.question: What is a 'Segmentation Fault' (SIGSEGV) in C programs?
questions.b: An operating system signal raised when a program attempts to access a memory address it does not have permission to read or write
questions.explanation: SIGSEGV is triggered by invalid memory accesses like dereferencing NULL or out-of-bounds writes.

questions.question: What is a 'Buffer Overflow' and why is it a critical security risk?
questions.a: When a program writes data beyond the allocated boundary of a buffer, corrupting adjacent stack memory or return addresses
questions.b: When the hard drive fills up completely
questions.c: When video graphics buffer runs out of VRAM
questions.d: When too many print statements execute
questions.explanation: Buffer overflows can overwrite stack frames and enable arbitrary code execution exploits.

questions.question: What tool is widely used on Linux to detect memory leaks, uninitialized memory reads, and out-of-bounds heap accesses in C programs?
questions.b: Valgrind (Memcheck)
questions.explanation: Valgrind Memcheck dynamically detects heap memory leaks, invalid frees, and memory corruptions.

questions.question: What does the GCC flag '-Wall -Wextra -Werror' do during compilation?
questions.b: Enables all comprehensive warnings and treats all warnings as fatal errors, enforcing clean code standards
questions.c: Generates release binaries without debugging symbols
questions.explanation: Enabling strict warning flags catches subtle bugs, uninitialized variables, and type mismatches.

questions.question: What is a 'Makefile' in software engineering?
questions.a: A text file containing build targets, dependencies, and shell compiler rules executed by the 'make' automation utility
questions.b: A file containing raw machine code
questions.explanation: Makefiles automate modular compilation based on file modification timestamps.

questions.question: What is the difference between static linking and dynamic linking in C?
questions.a: Static linking bundles library code directly into the executable binary; dynamic linking links shared libraries (.so/.dll) at runtime
questions.b: Static linking only works on Windows
questions.c: Dynamic linking is slower to write
questions.explanation: Static binaries are self-contained; dynamic binaries share library memory across running processes.

questions.question: What is the 'Stack' vs 'Heap' memory in C program architecture?
questions.a: Stack is automatically managed fast memory for local function variables; Heap is manually managed dynamic memory for lifetime-controlled allocations
questions.b: Stack is stored on disk; Heap is stored in CPU cache
questions.c: Stack is unlimited; Heap is 1 MB
questions.d: There is no difference in architecture
questions.explanation: Stack frames are managed by function calls/returns; heap memory is allocated/freed manually via malloc/free.

questions.question: What does the 'volatile' type qualifier tell the C compiler?
questions.a: The variable can never be changed
questions.b: The variable may be modified unexpectedly by external hardware or concurrent threads, preventing compiler optimization caching
questions.c: The variable is stored on the GPU
questions.explanation: volatile forces direct memory reads/writes every time, bypassing register caching in memory-mapped I/O.

questions.question: In memory segment architecture of a C process, what is the 'BSS' (Block Started by Symbol) segment used for?
questions.b: Storing uninitialized global and static variables (zero-initialized by the OS at startup)
questions.d: Storing command-line arguments and environment variables
questions.explanation: The BSS segment stores uninitialized global and static variables; the OS maps it to zeroed pages without taking file space in the binary.

questions.question: In process memory layout, what is the 'Text' (or Code) segment?
questions.a: The area storing string literals and printf outputs
questions.b: The read-only memory segment containing compiled machine code instructions
questions.c: The heap storage for character arrays
questions.d: The stack frames for text formatting functions
questions.explanation: The Text segment contains the executable CPU instructions of the program, marked read-only to prevent self-modification.

questions.question: In which direction does the call stack typically grow on most modern x86 and ARM computer architectures?
questions.a: From low memory addresses toward high memory addresses
questions.b: From high memory addresses downward toward low memory addresses
questions.explanation: On x86/x64 and ARM, the call stack grows downward (from higher memory addresses to lower addresses) toward the heap.

questions.question: What is 'Little-Endian' byte order in computer architecture?
questions.a: The most significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address
questions.b: The least significant byte (LSB) is stored at the lowest memory address
questions.c: Bytes are stored in inverted bit order
questions.d: Bytes are compressed using Huffman encoding
questions.explanation: Little-endian architectures (such as x86/x64 and ARM) store the least significant byte at the lowest memory address.

questions.question: What is 'Big-Endian' (Network Byte Order)?
questions.a: The least significant byte is stored first
questions.b: The most significant byte (MSB) is stored at the lowest memory address
questions.c: All numbers are converted to 64 bits
questions.explanation: Big-endian stores the most significant byte first (at the lowest address), which is standard for TCP/IP network protocols.

questions.question: Which functions convert 16-bit and 32-bit integers between Host Byte Order and Network Byte Order in socket programming?
questions.b: byte_swap16() / byte_swap32()
questions.explanation: htons/htonl (Host to Network Short/Long) and ntohs/ntohl (Network to Host Short/Long) convert integer byte order portably.

questions.question: What is the role of the 'Linker' (ld) in the C compilation toolchain?
questions.a: It converts C source code into assembly language
questions.b: It combines multiple compiled object files (.o) and libraries into a single executable binary, resolving external symbol references
questions.c: It expands macros and header files
questions.explanation: The linker combines compiled object files, resolves cross-file function/variable symbols, and produces the executable.

questions.question: What does the compiler optimization flag '-O2' or '-O3' instruct GCC/Clang to do?
questions.b: Apply aggressive optimizations (inlining, loop unrolling, vectorization) to increase runtime execution speed
questions.d: Enforce strict ISO C syntax mode
questions.explanation: -O2 and -O3 enable extensive performance optimizations including auto-vectorization, instruction scheduling, and function inlining.

questions.question: What is an 'Object File' (.o or .obj) produced by a C compiler?
questions.a: A JSON file containing code metadata
questions.b: A binary file containing unlinked machine code instructions and relocation symbols generated from a single translation unit
questions.d: A backup copy of the C header
questions.explanation: Object files contain compiled machine code with unresolved symbol tables, ready to be linked into a final executable or library.

questions.question: What is a 'Core Dump' file generated by the operating system upon a crash?
questions.a: A dump of the entire hard drive contents
questions.b: A snapshot of the program's memory space and CPU register state at the moment of fatal termination, used for post-mortem debugging in GDB
questions.explanation: A core dump records the process state (stack, registers, heap) at the moment of abnormal termination for diagnostic analysis in debuggers like GDB.

questions.question: What is the exact result of executing: int a = 5; int b = a++ + ++a; in ISO C?
questions.a: Always exactly 12 across all standard compilers
questions.b: Always exactly 13 across all standard compilers
questions.c: Undefined behavior due to multiple unsequenced modifications
questions.d: Compile-time syntax error on arithmetic addition
questions.explanation: Modifying a scalar object more than once between sequence points without intervening sequencing invokes Undefined Behavior (UB).

questions.question: Consider char *p = "hello"; p[0] = 'H';. What happens at runtime on modern operating systems?
questions.a: p[0] becomes 'H' successfully in read-write memory
questions.b: Segmentation fault / bus error writing to read-only string literal
questions.c: String is copied to stack automatically before modification
questions.d: Compiler truncates the string to single character 'H'
questions.explanation: String literals are stored in read-only text/data sections. Attempting to mutate them via char* causes a segmentation fault.

questions.question: What does the declaration void (*signal(int sig, void (*func)(int)))(int); define?
questions.a: A pointer to an array of function pointers returning integers
questions.b: A function taking int and func pointer, returning a func pointer
questions.c: A recursive macro expanding to POSIX signal handler prototypes
questions.d: A syntax error under ANSI C89 and modern C99 compilers
questions.explanation: signal is a function accepting an int and a function pointer (taking int, returning void), which returns a pointer to a function taking int and returning void.

questions.question: What is the strict aliasing rule in C (ISO C99 Section 6.5)?
questions.a: Pointers of different types cannot point to the same memory unless one is char*
questions.b: Two pointer variables cannot share the same variable identifier name
questions.c: Struct members must align strictly to 64-bit boundaries in heap memory
questions.d: Functions cannot accept both float and double pointer parameters together
questions.explanation: Strict aliasing states that two pointers of incompatible types cannot alias the same memory (with exceptions like char* and compatible signed/unsigned types), enabling aggressive compiler optimizations.

questions.question: What does free(ptr) do to the address stored inside the pointer variable ptr itself?
questions.a: Automatically assigns NULL to ptr in caller scope
questions.b: Leaves ptr holding the deallocated memory address (dangling pointer)
questions.c: Zeroes the 8 bytes of stack storage where ptr lives
questions.d: Deallocates ptr variable stack storage immediately
questions.explanation: free() receives the pointer address by value and releases the heap chunk. It cannot modify the caller pointer variable, leaving it dangling.

questions.question: What is 'Undefined Behavior' (UB) in the ISO C standard?
questions.b: Code execution for which the C standard imposes no requirements; the program may crash, produce garbage output, or appear to work unpredictably
questions.c: A feature reserved for future C versions
questions.explanation: UB allows compilers to assume illegal conditions never occur, leading to aggressive optimizations and unpredictable bugs.

questions.question: What is the 'Strict Aliasing Rule' in C?
questions.a: Pointers of different incompatible types cannot point to the same memory location, allowing compilers to assume their dereferences do not interfere
questions.b: Variables must have unique names
questions.d: Pointers cannot be cast to void *
questions.explanation: Strict aliasing permits register caching by assuming different type pointers do not alias the same memory.

questions.question: What does AddressSanitizer (ASan) flag '-fsanitize=address' do when compiling with modern GCC/Clang?
questions.b: Instruments compiled code with fast memory error detection for out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and stack bugs
questions.explanation: ASan detects memory safety violations at runtime with minimal performance overhead.

questions.question: What is a 'Race Condition' in multi-threaded C programming using POSIX threads (pthread)?
questions.a: A competition between two CPU cores
questions.b: When two or more concurrent threads access shared memory simultaneously and at least one access is a write without synchronization (mutex)
questions.c: When a loop runs faster than expected
questions.explanation: Data races corrupt shared state; mutex locks or atomic operations are required to serialize access.

questions.question: What does the 'restrict' keyword (introduced in C99) signify when qualifying a pointer parameter?
questions.b: The pointer is the sole exclusive reference to the object it points to within that scope, enabling aggressive compiler vectorization
questions.c: The pointer cannot be passed to other functions
questions.d: The pointer is allocated on stack
questions.explanation: restrict informs the optimizer that no other pointer will access the same memory block.

questions.question: What is an 'Atomic Operation' in concurrent C programming (stdatomic.h)?
questions.a: An operation that uses nuclear computing
questions.b: An indivisible memory read-modify-write operation that executes completely without possibility of interruption or data race from other threads
questions.explanation: Atomic instructions execute as a single indivisible hardware step without mutex locking.

questions.question: Why is modifying a global variable inside an asynchronous Signal Handler considered hazardous in C?
questions.a: Signals can interrupt execution at any instruction; non-atomic signal modifications cause data corruption unless typed as 'volatile sig_atomic_t'
questions.b: Signal handlers cannot access memory
questions.explanation: Only async-signal-safe functions and volatile sig_atomic_t variables can be safely modified in signal handlers.

questions.question: What is 'Memory Alignment' and why does unaligned memory access cause performance penalties or hardware faults on ARM/MIPS CPUs?
questions.a: CPUs fetch data in multi-byte word chunks; accessing data across word boundaries requires multiple memory bus cycles or triggers hardware alignment faults
questions.b: Memory must be arranged alphabetically
questions.d: Unaligned access causes hard drive fragmentation
questions.explanation: CPUs access memory efficiently when addresses are multiples of natural data sizes (2, 4, 8 bytes).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'setjmp()' and 'longjmp()' functions in <setjmp.h>?
questions.a: To allocate jump tables in heap
questions.b: To perform non-local jumps (unwinding stack frames across functions) for low-level exception handling and error recovery
questions.explanation: setjmp saves execution context and longjmp restores it, jumping across stack frames.

questions.question: What is a 'Zero-Day Vulnerability' frequently rooted in C memory unsafety?
questions.a: A bug that takes 0 days to fix
questions.b: A previously unknown software security flaw (such as a remote heap buffer overflow or use-after-free) exploited before developers release a patch
questions.explanation: C memory safety vulnerabilities are prime targets for zero-day remote code execution exploits.

questions.question: What is 'Type Punning' via unions in C99/C11?
questions.b: Writing data to one member of a union and reading it back through another member of a different type to inspect raw representation
questions.c: Converting floating point numbers to strings
questions.d: Bypassing function return types using void*
questions.explanation: In C (unlike C++), reading from a different union member than the one last written to is standard-approved for type punning.

questions.question: What does the C11 '_Generic' keyword enable in C?
questions.b: Compile-time type-generic macro selection based on the type of an expression
questions.explanation: _Generic (introduced in C11) provides compile-time function overloading / selection based on argument types (used in <tgmath.h>).

questions.question: What does the 'static_assert()' macro (or _Static_assert in C11) do?
questions.a: Performs runtime checking of assertion statements
questions.b: Tests a boolean condition at compile time and emits a compilation error if false
questions.c: Asserts that a function is static
questions.d: Freezes static variables from further modifications
questions.explanation: static_assert performs compile-time verification of constant expressions (e.g. verifying struct sizes or platform bit-widths).

questions.question: What is an 'Async-Signal-Safe' function in C POSIX standards?
questions.a: A function that can be safely invoked inside an asynchronous signal handler without risking deadlock or state corruption
questions.b: A function running on a background worker thread
questions.c: A function that ignores all OS termination signals
questions.d: A function that sends asynchronous network packets
questions.explanation: Async-signal-safe functions (like write()) are guaranteed reentrant and safe to call from interrupt handlers; functions like printf() and malloc() are unsafe.

questions.question: What is the 'ThreadSanitizer' (TSan) compiler flag '-fsanitize=thread' used for?
questions.b: Detecting multithreaded data races and deadlocks at runtime
questions.explanation: TSan instruments memory accesses to detect data races where two threads access shared memory without synchronization.

questions.question: What does the 'UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer' (UBSan) flag '-fsanitize=undefined' detect?
questions.b: Runtime undefined behaviors such as signed integer overflow, misaligned pointers, null pointer dereferences, and invalid shifts
questions.explanation: UBSan instruments binaries to detect runtime undefined behaviors like signed overflow, zero division, and misaligned pointer dereferences.

questions.question: What is 'Memory Compaction' vs 'External Memory Fragmentation' in custom heap allocators in C?
questions.b: External fragmentation occurs when total free memory is sufficient but split into non-contiguous blocks too small to satisfy an allocation
questions.c: Memory compaction is handled automatically by hardware L1 cache
questions.d: External fragmentation only affects stack memory
questions.explanation: External fragmentation leaves free memory scattered in small chunks, preventing large contiguous allocations.

questions.question: What is a 'Spinlock' in multi-core concurrent C programming?
questions.a: A mutex that puts waiting threads to sleep immediately
questions.b: A lock mechanism where a thread repeatedly checks a shared atomic flag in a tight loop until it becomes available
questions.c: A lock that rotates between threads in round-robin fashion
questions.d: A hardware failure in CPU cooling fans
questions.explanation: A spinlock polls an atomic condition in a tight loop, ideal for very short critical sections where context switching overhead is undesirable.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'Memory Barriers' (or Memory Fences, e.g. atomic_thread_fence) in concurrent C?
questions.a: To prevent unauthorized users from reading RAM
questions.b: To enforce ordering constraints on memory operations preventing compiler and CPU out-of-order reordering
questions.c: To create guard pages around stack frames
questions.d: To block network packets at the OS level
questions.explanation: Memory fences enforce strict memory access ordering across multi-core processors, preventing hardware/compiler reordering across threads.

questions.question: What is a 'False Sharing' performance bug in multi-threaded C applications?
questions.b: Different threads modifying independent variables that reside on the same CPU cache line (e.g. 64 bytes), causing constant cache invalidation
questions.explanation: False sharing occurs when independent variables share a single cache line, causing cache-coherency invalidations between CPU cores.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'Valgrind Memcheck' tool in C development on Linux?
questions.b: Detecting memory leaks, invalid heap reads/writes, use-after-free, and uninitialized variable reads through CPU emulation
questions.explanation: Valgrind memcheck runs binaries in a synthetic CPU environment to track memory allocations and detect safety violations.

questions.question: What is a 'Stack Canary' inserted by modern compilers (-fstack-protector)?
questions.a: A secret security token placed on the stack before the return address to detect stack buffer overflows before returning
questions.b: A debugging function that logs stack depth
questions.c: An encrypted backup of the heap
questions.d: A tool for converting recursion to iteration
questions.explanation: A stack canary is a guard value placed on the stack; if corrupted by a buffer overflow, the program aborts immediately before hijacking control flow.

questions.question: What is 'Return-Oriented Programming' (ROP) in binary exploitation of C applications?
questions.a: Writing code purely using return statements
questions.b: An exploit technique that chains small snippets of existing machine instructions ending in 'ret' (gadgets) to bypass non-executable stack (DEP/NX) protection
questions.c: An optimization that removes function calls
questions.explanation: ROP bypasses data execution prevention (DEP/NX) by executing existing snippets of code ("gadgets") already present in executable memory.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) in modern operating systems running C executables?
questions.a: Randomizing variable values for cryptographic simulations
questions.b: Randomizing the memory addresses of the stack, heap, and shared libraries at launch to make return-to-libc and ROP exploits unpredictable
questions.c: Distributing memory allocations across RAM chips randomly
questions.explanation: ASLR randomizes memory layout offsets, making fixed-address memory corruption exploits significantly harder to execute.

questions.question: What does the C99 'inline' keyword combined with 'extern' vs 'static' in header files govern?
questions.b: Whether the compiler emits a callable external symbol definition in the translation unit or strictly inlines the function body
questions.explanation: In C99, 'static inline' guarantees internal linkage with inlining, whereas 'extern inline' provides an inline definition while emitting an external symbol elsewhere.
